entry.title: How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation
entry.summary: 'Hexed' writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller and directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad tell IndieWire about their latest Disney film.
entry.content:
Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen.

Related Stories
How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?
Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap
entry.summary: Netflix's camp comedy and conservative satire 'The Hunting Wives' pulls Sophie (Brittany Snow) and Margo (Malin Åkerman) together again. [REVIEW]
entry.content:
Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

Just kill ’em.

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours!

Related Stories
‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down
Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

Grade: B

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

entry.title: How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?
entry.summary: Parallels between the two projects are obvious, so allow us to speculate on where on script ended and another began.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.”

Related Stories
Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It
Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

entry.title: Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It
entry.summary: 'I Swear' star Robert Aramayo nabbed two BAFTAs at this year's fraught ceremony, but as he tells IndieWire, the next step isn't just more glory.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan).

Related Stories
‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down
Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”

[Laughs]

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

entry.title: ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down
entry.summary: Ethan Hawke wants to nominate Peter Dinklage in 'The Lowdown' Season 2 finale for an Oscar: 'It was like, Let me show you kids how to do a poem!'
entry.content:
[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.]

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter.

Related Stories
Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’
Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke said. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”

“And that’s what I did. It has this bit of nostalgia. It also has this magic to it and this dreamlike quality to what he’s doing,” Harjo said. “The character is such an internal person that the only way you’re going to get those monologues is through a journal when he thinks it’s the privacy of himself and his journal. He’s expressing things that he wouldn’t normally express out loud.”

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke said. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo said. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

entry.title: Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’
entry.summary: Oscar nominee Danielle Brooks shares how she and the other 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' filmmakers found true independent success.
entry.content:
“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.”

Related Stories
What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?
‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

entry.title: What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?
entry.summary: From "Blood Rage" to "The Last Waltz," independent movie theaters across America are bringing audiences together with special Thanksgiving screenings.
entry.content:
One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism.

Related Stories
‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?
Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

entry.title: Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season
entry.summary: The Will Ferrell golf comedy 'The Hawk' was canceled at Netflix after just one season.
entry.content:
“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and big mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.”

Related Stories
Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?
‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three new series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

entry.title: ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?
entry.summary: Writer/director Ryūsuke Hamaguchi on why the capitalism-vs-nature whiteboard seminar works cinematically and was so important to his film.
entry.content:
It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.

Related Stories
Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out
‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” said Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”

The scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her new companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

“I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” said Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very important and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

To hear Ryūsuke Hamaguchi’s full interview, subscribe to the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast on Apple, Spotify, or your favorite podcast platform. You can also watch the full interview on YouTube

entry.title: Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Craft Roundtables, Graham Page explained the detailed research that made his animated sheep so lifelike.
entry.content:
It’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike.

Related Stories
‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy
IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

“To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”
